seoTitle: Michigan Drunk Driving Accident Lawyer – Victims’ Claims & Dram Shop
seoDescription: Hit by a drunk driver in Michigan? You may have claims against the driver and the bar that served them, with a 120-day notice rule. ATLAW explains both, plus restitution. Free review.
tagline: Two claims, not one: the driver, and the bar or store that served them. The second has a deadline measured in days.

c.v: If you were hit by a drunk driver in Michigan, you have the claim everyone expects, against the driver, and often a second claim most people never hear about, against the bar, restaurant, or store that served the driver while visibly intoxicated. Michigan’s dram shop law makes that seller liable. It also imposes a written-notice deadline of 120 days from the day you hire a lawyer, and a rule that the drunk driver must be kept in the case as a defendant. A victim who waits six months to call a lawyer has usually lost the second claim without knowing it existed.
This page explains both claims, how the criminal case against the driver helps you, what no-fault pays, and the deadlines.

sections.heading: The claim against the drunk driver

c.v: A drunk driver is a negligent driver with the fault question already answered. Michigan’s drunk driving law (MCL 257.625) makes it a crime to operate with a blood alcohol content of 0.08 or more, with enhanced penalties at 0.17 (“high BAC”), and a zero-tolerance rule for drivers under 21 that can apply even below 0.02. Operating while intoxicated and causing a serious injury is a felony punishable by up to five years; causing a death, up to fifteen (MCL 257.625(4), (5)).

In your civil case, the driver’s intoxication is evidence of negligence, and a conviction or guilty plea is admissible. Michigan no-fault still applies: your own insurer pays your medical bills and 85% of lost wages (up to $7,455 a month for crashes on or after October 1, 2026) regardless of fault, with written notice within one year (MCL 500.3145). You sue the driver for pain and suffering and for economic losses beyond no-fault if your injury is a serious impairment of body function (MCL 500.3135), which crash injuries caused by an impaired driver usually are.
Two points specific to drunk driving cases:
Michigan does not award punitive damages

items.v: in negligence cases, including drunk driving cases, whatever other states’ websites say. The driver’s conduct bears on how a jury values your pain and suffering; there is no separate penalty award.

c.v: The driver’s policy is often the problem.

items.v: Drunk drivers carry minimum coverage ($50,000 per person) or none, and insurers sometimes dispute coverage for criminal conduct. Your own uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage, and the dram shop claim, are how serious injuries are compensated when the driver’s policy runs out.

sections.heading: The claim against the bar: Michigan’s dram shop law

c.v: Michigan’s Liquor Control Code (MCL 436.1801) prohibits a licensed retailer, meaning a bar, restaurant, party store, or any business licensed to sell alcohol, from selling or serving alcohol to a minor or to a visibly intoxicated person. If it does, and the sale is a proximate cause of a crash, the person injured by the intoxicated driver (or the family, in a death) has a direct claim against the retailer.
The elements:
A licensed retailer sold or served alcohol

items.v: to the driver. The law applies to licensees; a private host who served an adult guest is not liable (see below).

c.v: The driver was visibly intoxicated at the time

items.v: , or was under 21. “Visibly” is the fight in most cases: slurred speech, stumbling, glassy eyes, the number of drinks served, how long they were there, what the bartender and other patrons saw. Bar surveillance video, receipts, and tab records are the evidence, and they are overwritten or discarded within weeks.

c.v: The sale was a proximate cause

items.v: of the intoxication and the crash.

c.v: The rules that make dram shop claims different from every other injury claim:
Written notice within 120 days.

items.v: The injured person must give written notice to every retailer they intend to sue within 120 days after retaining an attorney, unless they can show they did not know and could not reasonably have known who the retailer was (MCL 436.1801(4)). Missing it is grounds for dismissal.

c.v: Two years to sue.

items.v: A dram shop claim must be filed within two years of the injury (MCL 436.1801(3)), not the three years that applies to the claim against the driver.

c.v: Name and retain.

items.v: The intoxicated driver must be named as a defendant and kept in the lawsuit through judgment or settlement (MCL 436.1801(4)). A victim who settles with the driver and releases them first has, in most cases, lost the dram shop claim.

c.v: The last sale presumption.

items.v: When the driver drank at more than one place, the law presumes that only the retailer that made the last sale is responsible, and the others must be shown to have served the driver while visibly intoxicated (MCL 436.1801(7)).

c.v: The drunk driver cannot sue the bar

items.v: for their own injuries (MCL 436.1801(8)). The claim belongs to the people they hurt.

c.v: A dram shop defendant is a business with liquor liability insurance, which is why the claim matters: it is often the only policy large enough to compensate a catastrophic injury or a death.
Social hosts.
A private individual who serves alcohol to an adult guest who then drives drunk is not liable under Michigan law. A social host who furnishes alcohol to a
minor

is: furnishing alcohol to a minor is a crime (MCL 436.1701), and Michigan courts allow the minor’s victims to sue the adult who provided it. House parties, graduation parties, and the parents who supplied the alcohol are the typical case.

sections.heading: How the criminal case helps your claim

c.v: A drunk driver who hurts someone is prosecuted by the county, and the victim has rights in that case under Michigan’s Crime Victim’s Rights Act: to be notified of hearings, to be consulted on a plea, to give a victim impact statement at sentencing, and to
restitution

. Under MCL 780.766, the sentencing court must order the defendant to pay full restitution to the victim for the losses the crime caused: medical expenses, lost income, property damage, counseling, and funeral costs. Restitution is a court order enforceable like a judgment, independent of insurance.

The criminal file is also evidence for the civil case: the blood or breath test result, the officer’s observations, the body camera footage, and, in a plea, an admission of intoxication. We obtain all of it. The civil case does not wait for the criminal case to end, but the two are coordinated.

faqs.question: Can I sue the bar that served the drunk driver?

answer.v: Yes, under Michigan’s dram shop law (MCL 436.1801), if the bar, restaurant, or store served the driver while visibly intoxicated or under 21, and the sale was a cause of the crash. You must give the bar written notice within 120 days of hiring a lawyer and sue within two years.

That the driver showed signs of intoxication a server would have noticed: slurred speech, unsteadiness, loud or erratic behavior, the number and pace of drinks. It is proven with surveillance video, receipts, witnesses, and the driver’s BAC worked backward.

faqs.question: Can I settle with the drunk driver and still sue the bar?

answer.v: Not safely. The dram shop law requires the drunk driver to be named and kept as a defendant in the case. Releasing the driver before the dram shop claim is resolved usually ends it. Talk to a lawyer before accepting anything.

faqs.question: Can I get punitive damages from a drunk driver in Michigan?

answer.v: No. Michigan does not award punitive damages in negligence cases. The driver’s conduct affects how a jury values your pain and suffering, and the criminal court can order restitution, but there is no separate penalty award.

A court order in the criminal case requiring the convicted driver to pay your losses: medical bills, lost wages, property damage, counseling, funeral costs (MCL 780.766). It is enforceable like a judgment and does not depend on insurance.

faqs.question: Does no-fault still pay if the other driver was drunk?

answer.v: Yes. Your own insurer pays your medical bills and wage loss regardless of fault. The drunk driver and the dram shop defendant are liable for pain and suffering and the rest.

faqs.question: What if the drunk driver had no insurance?

answer.v: Your uninsured motorist coverage (if you bought it) pays what the driver’s insurer would have. The dram shop claim, if there is one, is often the larger source of recovery. Restitution applies regardless.

faqs.question: What if I was a passenger in the drunk driver’s car?

answer.v: You can claim against the driver’s policy and, if the driver was served while visibly intoxicated, against the bar. The insurer will argue you assumed the risk by riding with an impaired driver; that is a comparative-fault argument, not a bar to the claim.

faqs.question: What if the driver was high, not drunk?

answer.v: Operating under the influence of marijuana or drugs is treated the same way for your civil claim: evidence of negligence, no-fault still applies, serious impairment threshold for the lawsuit. The dram shop law applies only to alcohol.

faqs.question: How much does a drunk driving accident lawyer cost?
